1:
Whether the opening words are an oath divides them. Henry says they are in the form of an oath, an appeal to what the readers themselves hope for: if they believe Christ will come and rejoice in that hope, they should avoid this error. Calvin agrees it is an earnest entreaty, since it is customary to adjure by what we regard with reverence, and thinks the adjuration itself teaches us to think of that day only with reverence and sobriety. Ellicott sharpens the preposition, not the simple by but for the sake of, a stronger form implying that the thing adjured by will suffer if the request is refused: the coming and the meeting with the beloved dead would not be so bright, so perfect, perhaps so soon, if they were misled. Barnes denies the whole construction. The phrase is no adjuration, since Scripture does not adjure in view of an event; it means simply concerning his coming.

On the gathering together, Robertson notes the noun is late and rare, found in the Maccabees, in one other place in the epistles, and on a stone in the island of Syme meaning a collection; he takes it of the rapture described in the earlier letter. Ellicott observes that the one other occurrence is used of assembling for the Lord's Supper, so some read it in that sense here, and takes the possessive of the meeting of the dead and the living together. Henry makes the point devotionally: all the saints of both testaments will be gathered, and gathered to Christ as the centre of their unity.

The verb for shaken is read as a sea word: Barnes takes it of a wave, or a vessel tossed upon the waves; Clarke of a ship agitated in a storm, marking the confusion the readers felt; Ellicott would insert a so before soon, since the point is not that they should never be shaken but that they had been shaken already, in an unconscionably short time since they were first taught. He distinguishes the tenses too, the driving out of their wits a single act, the trouble a chronic condition they were in danger of falling into. Barnes adds a modern instance, that in a single year seventeen persons were admitted to one asylum whose minds had given way under the expectation that the Lord was about to appear.

What misled them is disputed. Barnes gives three reasons for a letter forged in the apostles' name rather than the earlier letter misread: the qualifying as from us would be needless of his own writing, the warning that no man deceive them implies a deliberate attempt rather than a misreading, and forged epistles were common in the early centuries. Clarke declines to choose and joins both senses, the former letter, some passages of which had been misconceived, and any other letter pretending to be from the apostles. Ellicott takes the qualifying phrase with the spoken word too, so that some had misrepresented what they had heard said. Gill and Henry keep to misunderstanding, Henry allowing that some may have pretended a private revelation.

Calvin looks behind the error to its use. Some disposed to indulge curiosity philosophised unseasonably about the time once the first letter had been read; and this was Satan's subtlety, that being unable to overturn the hope of a resurrection openly he undermined it by promising a near day, since when a day named does not quickly arrive men grow impatient, their spirits languish, and languishing is shortly followed by despair. He instances the dreams of Lactantius and the old Chiliasts, which delighted the multitude yet tended only to overthrow the hope they seemed to serve. Clarke raises the question that governs everything after, whether the coming meant is the judgment on the Jewish polity or the end of the world, and answers that the prophecy has both in view, neither exclusively.
3:
The warning is wide. Robertson says the caution goes beyond conversation and letter to tricks of any kind, and remarks how gullible some saints are when a new deceiver pulls off some stunts; what follows means the coming is not merely not imminent but cannot occur until certain things have happened. Much turns on an article. Ellicott says a great change is felt as soon as the is put for a, since the purpose is not to utter a new prophecy but to recall teaching given in the first weeks after their conversion; that falling away must mean the apostates once held the Christian faith, for men cannot fall from ground they never occupied. Barnes reports Erasmus to the same effect, that the article signifies the great and before-predicted apostasy. Clarke defines the word as a dereliction of the essential principles of religious truth, either a total abandonment of Christianity or such a corruption of its doctrines as leaves the system inefficient to salvation, and adds that what it means is a question which has not yet, and perhaps never will be, answered to general satisfaction.

The two surveys of the identifications largely agree. Between them Barnes and Clarke record: a defection under persecution between Nero and Trajan; a return of converts to Judaism before Jerusalem fell, with the Jewish nation as the man of sin; the Gnostic defection, with Simon Magus; Caligula, whose iniquity was concealed early and afterwards revealed; Titus and the Flavian house, on the ground that the Roman pontiff neither sits in the temple nor calls himself God; the king of Daniel's eleventh chapter; the rabbinic and Pharisaic system; Mohammed; Napoleon; someone not yet appeared at all; and, from most Protestant writers, the papacy and the succession of popes.

The protest against that last reading is recorded too. Clarke reports Calmet following the ancient fathers and wondering at the want of candour in Protestant writers who have gleaned up every abusive tale against the bishops and Church of Rome, asking whether they would be willing that Catholics should credit all the aspersions cast on Protestantism. Barnes states a method rather than assert a conclusion: eighteen hundred years have passed and the day has not come, so we judge in better circumstances than those who succeeded the apostles; if the description fairly fits one great apostasy and can fit nothing else, it is proper to apply it there, and if not, we must wait for its fulfilment.

Whether one man or a line is meant is argued from the prophets. Barnes holds it a succession, since a king in Daniel stands for a line of kings, the beast for an empire through its revolutions, and the woman in scarlet for a continued administration, and the work assigned could not be finished by one man, revealed early and yet continuing until the coming. Ellicott allows the phrase might personify a movement, but thinks the analogy of Daniel points rather to an actual individual impersonating it, and insists the man of sin is the head and centre of the apostasy and not separate from it, so that no reading will do which makes the two independent.

The titles are pressed for their force. Ellicott takes the genitive as a forcible epithet, a man so wicked that wickedness is his distinguishing mark, in whom the ideal of sin has become incarnate, the crowning sin being spiritual pride and rebellious arrogancy; and the word for his revealing is the one used of Christ, so that Antichrist is not merely an opponent but a rival, with a hideous parallelism between the two. Clarke matches the second title to Judas, and finds the rabbis giving the same names to Adam after his fall. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies a mechanism: hatred of the brethren makes room for Antichrist, the devil preparing the divisions so that he who is to come may be acceptable.
4:
The epithets are read as one portrait. Ellicott notes the Greek keeps a substantival form, the opposer and self-exalter, and that the first word closely renders the name Satan and became a synonym for it, though minister and master are not to be confounded; he corrects the second, since above belongs with the verb: super-exalts himself against every God so called, while the opposing stands absolutely, this figure being always in opposition, with concord for no one. Calvin uses the epithets structurally: they set this kingdom in direct opposition to the kingdom of Christ, and since Christ's kingdom is spiritual this tyranny must be over souls to rival it, so that to know Antichrist you must view him as diametrically opposed to Christ.

On the words as God the witnesses run one way. Clarke reports them wanting in the chief uncials and in the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate, and in most Greek fathers, notes that Griesbach dropped them, quotes an editor saying they should most certainly be erased, and thinks the text reads better without them. Barnes agrees there is much reason to doubt them, asterisked in the Vulgate, Coptic and Syriac, rejected by Griesbach and Lachmann, though defended by four editors he names; the sense, he adds, is not materially affected. Ellicott says they are no part of the original text and should be struck out. Calvin raises another variant, thinking a transcriber mistook one letter for a similar one, turning all that is called God into every God.

What temple is meant divides them. Barnes takes it of the Christian church as a society, not the building at Jerusalem, since the phrase is used of the church elsewhere; the reign described would be as if this figure sat where God sat, giving laws and receiving homage. Ellicott presses the word, not the whole group of buildings but the sacred house itself, so that the Holy of Holies is meant and probably the Mercy Seat supplies the image; the tense marks one act of possession, the preposition an intrusion. Yet he denies a literal seat in that edifice was expected, or that the phrase is a mere synonym for the church, calling the whole a prophetical description of usurping divine prerogatives. Robertson brings in the emperor: Caligula made a desperate attempt to have his statue set up for worship in the temple at Jerusalem and claimed to be God, which may lie behind the language; one scholar thinks the deification of emperors supplied it, another doubts the identification.

Two apply the description to the papacy in detail. Barnes lists the claims: authority above every order of the priesthood; above kings and emperors, with Gregory making Henry wait barefooted at his gate and Celestin kicking off an imperial crown, and the apportioning of the new world; and over conscience, in infallibility, in forbidding what God allowed, and in remitting sins. He then quotes titles given the pope by Catholic writers without rebuke: his power extends to things celestial, terrestrial and infernal, and he does whatsoever he pleases, even things unlawful. Calvin argues from the other end, listing what Scripture reserves to God: the one lawgiver whose office is to govern souls by his word, the sole source of righteousness and salvation; there is not one of these the pope does not claim, so that in robbing God of his honour he leaves him nothing but an empty title of deity.

Ellicott draws a conclusion from the openness of the act. The claim being spontaneous and paraded, an explicit demand for the submission of creature to Creator seems implied; and since it is hard to believe anything avowedly atheistic would be spoken of as receiving divine honours, the great apostasy will probably not become atheistic at all, but will be an apostasy within the church, its head claiming from the church the very honours she pays to the living God.
5:
The appeal to what they had been told begins the difficulty. Barnes says much of the obscurity arises from an allusion to teaching of which we have no record, so that what would have been clear to the first readers is now hard to understand. Clarke adds that the writer speaks with great caution and does not wish to publish what he had said in private, the hints dropped being enough to recall the whole. Ellicott presses the tense, not a single act but a habit, my custom was to tell you these things, and notices that in this one recollection Silas and Timothy are forgotten and the pronoun becomes I: imagine, he says, a forger who should forge with such subtlety. Robertson admits the recollection leaves us without the clue; Calvin notes the mildness: it is a fatherly reproof to say only that they had let forgetfulness steal in upon a matter so useful.

Chrysostom states the question and answers it. Some say the grace of the Spirit withholds and others the Roman empire, and he accedes most of all to the second: if the Spirit were meant the writer would have said so plainly, and if the restraint were the gifts, long since ceased, the revealing ought already to have happened. The obscurity is then deliberate and prudent. He speaks covertly because he did not wish to bring on himself superfluous enmities and useless dangers: had he said openly that the Roman empire would shortly be dissolved, they would have overwhelmed him at once as a pestilent person, and all the faithful as living and warring to that end.

The later voices reach the same identification otherwise. Barnes notes the neuter in one verse and the masculine in the next, argues the restraint must be outside the church and distinct from the apostasy itself, and so takes it of civil power; he reports that the primitive Christians held it to be the Roman empire and prayed for its peace, knowing that when it broke the empire of the man of sin would rise on its ruins, and quotes a historian on the emperor quitting Rome for Constantinople, after which the empire declined while the church of Rome augmented as fast, until under the Lombards the pope, as governor of the city, began to hold up his head. Henry gives it in a sentence: the power supposed is the Roman empire, not named more plainly at the time. Ellicott adds a motive for the reticence: the withholder was present and tangible, not a dim figure of the future, and the writer may shrink from naming it for fear the power itself should discover and disapprove of his prophecies.

On the iniquity already at work Barnes is careful with the word, which means hidden rather than unintelligible: some concealed depravity operating silently in the church. He passes on one list of the seeds then present, the pride of ministers, the factious temper of Christians, unauthorised severities, and the worship of angels, and another adding idolatry stealing in, the adulterating of the word, teaching for filthy lucre, the vain observation of festivals and distinction of meats, and traditions of men. Bishop Newton's judgment, which he adopts, is that the foundations were laid in the apostles' days and the superstructure raised by degrees. Henry's account is the same: corruption of doctrine and worship came in by degrees and the usurping of power was gradual, and while the apostles yet lived men pretended zeal for Christ but really opposed him.

Robertson will not settle it. Unfortunately, he says, we do not know what is meant by that which restrains; he passes on the observation that an impersonal principle may also manifest itself under a personal form, the description of the figure as an infernal caricature of the true Messiah, and a suggestion that the imperial line with its rage for deification is meant.
8:
The change of title is noticed first. Ellicott says the English obscures the passage by not keeping the word used two verses earlier, since the tendency to lawlessness is here brought to a head in the Lawless One, as the obstruction was impersonated in the Obstructor; the only new information is the date, so the emphasis rests on the words and then. Robertson marks the same note of time: when the restrainer is taken out of the way, the man of sin will be revealed.

How he is destroyed divides them. Barnes offers two readings of the breath of his mouth: what the Redeemer speaks at his coming, or his truth already spoken, in which case the destruction may have begun long before he appears and be completed only at his advent; he grants the most obvious interpretation refers both clauses to the same period. Clarke will have only the gradual sense, since it is by the preaching of the truth that this power is exposed, so its death will not be sudden; and he takes the brightness itself of the manifestation of truth it had kept obscured. Ellicott finds the point of the borrowed phrase in the perfect ease of the destruction, absence of labour being what the figure marks; and he renders the second clause the appearing of his presence, since the mere fact of the true Christ showing himself reduces the false one to nothing, for when they stand face to face there will be no possibility of delusion any more. Barnes agrees the word means merely an appearing and carries no necessary idea of splendour, so the agency is not the brightness but himself. Robertson calls the whole a grand fiasco, and notes that this figure has his own presence and epiphany, so that the two coincide.

Calvin argues it from contraries. Since this power cannot stand except through the impostures of Satan, it must vanish as soon as Christ shines forth, for it reigns only in darkness and the dawn puts thick darkness to flight; and since Christ's kingdom consists of the doctrine of truth and the power of the Spirit, the rival must consist of false doctrine and pretended miracles.

The miracles are treated as counterfeits. Ellicott would let the word for lying govern all three nouns, giving all counterfeit power and signs and wonders, piled up to heighten the terror, signs attesting the doctrine and wonders keeping men spellbound; and he sets the parallel out plainly, that this figure like Christ has one to support him, Satan instead of God, and like Christ will have his miracles, but of trickery and not of truth. Robertson notes these are the same three words used of the miracles of Christ. Clarke keeps the distinction, that these are only appearances of what was real, while God sent real miracles, signs and wonders, such as Satan cannot produce. Barnes turns it on the papacy and lists the marvels claimed for it: the dissolving of a saint's blood, Pilate's stairs removed to Rome, the house of the Virgin transported to Italy, the change of bread and wine at a priest's pleasure.

On those deceived the two schools part. Ellicott insists the phrase describing them who perish contains no reference to predestination but merely describes the class, men in course of perishing as a matter of fact, and that the words mean the truth was offered and refused, not, as he says Calvinism would teach, that it was never given; the grace to love the truth comes with every new presentment of it, and to be too indolent to examine whether a thing be true is already to reject that love. Calvin, on the same clause, holds Satan's power so limited that he cannot injure the elect at all, and this power to have no strength except by permission, which he offers as a necessary consolation to the pious.
11:
The mechanism is described before it is defended. Ellicott says these verses do not repeat the two before, since there the danger was external and here the effect is on the men themselves: God takes from them, by his natural law, the power of discerning the true from the false, and so as it were actually deceives them. Every wilful sin does this double mischief, strengthening the temptation without and weakening the power to resist within; and he points to Ahab, who cared only for the pleasant and not the true, and was requited with a lying spirit to entice him. A terrible combination, he adds, when God and Satan are agreed to deceive a man, and yet an encouragement to see God using Satan for his own purposes.

How far God acts divides them. Barnes admits the agency is distinctly recognised, as elsewhere in Scripture respecting evil, but argues no positive influence need be supposed: the force of the language is met by supposing God withdrew all restraint and suffered men to show that they did not love the truth, since he often places men in circumstances that develop their own nature, and it cannot be shown wrong that he should. Gill will not have it a bare permission but a voluntary one, and guards it by a distinction: the efficacy of error is not a sin, of which God cannot be the author, but a punishment for sin, brought about partly by his denying grace and withholding the light by which error might be detected. Calvin is the most positive. As God enlightens us inwardly by his Spirit and opens our eyes that his doctrine may find its way in, so by a righteous judgment he delivers over to a reprobate mind those he has appointed to destruction, that with closed eyes they may as if bewitched deliver themselves to Satan and his ministers to be deceived. Robertson calls it simply the definite judicial act of God, who gives the wicked over to the evil they have deliberately chosen.

Three details of the Greek are pressed. Ellicott notes the tense is present, sendeth rather than shall send, the writer seeing it before his eyes; that the phrase is better rendered an effectual inward working of error, no longer indifference to truth but a real influence of error on the heart; and that the lie carries the article, the particular lie they are to be made to believe. Clarke keeps the milder verb, that God permits the delusion to occupy their minds, so they are ever ready to receive any false Christ while rejecting the true.

The particle in the next verse is the sharpest disagreement. Ellicott reads it as purpose: this, he says, is God's design in making them believe the lie, that one and all they might be judged. Barnes denies the word must carry purpose, since it may mark only result and in later Greek may merely point back to what precedes; the passage teaches that such would be the outcome and the connection between delusion and condemnation is certain, but it cannot be proved that God sends men strong delusions in order that they may be damned, and no passage should be so construed if it can be avoided.

On the grounds of the sentence they agree. Barnes states two, that they did not believe the truth and that they had pleasure in unrighteousness, and holds there can be no juster ground than that a man loves to do wrong. Clarke says the same more briefly: their condemnation was the effect of their refusal to believe, and they refused because they loved their sins. Calvin points to a specimen he takes to be already visible, a monstrous nest of errors and delusions at variance with common sense, which none with even a moderate taste of sound doctrine can think of without horror.
13:
The turn to thanksgiving is read as deliberate relief. Ellicott calls it a recurrence to the subject dropped at the opening of the letter, and notes the delicacy: it would have been more natural to begin but you, and instead the writer describes the effect on himself and his companions of observing the difference. He presses two words. The participle rendered beloved makes the reader think of the everlasting duration of that love, and the substitution of the Lord for God shows the concurrence of the Son in the Father's predestinations; the verb should be rendered chose, referring to the definite moment in the divine counsels when the choice was fixed. Henry finds the consolation in the same place: when we hear of the apostasy of many it is great comfort that there is a remnant according to the election of grace which does and shall persevere, especially if we may hope we are of that number.

Barnes draws four propositions from the one clause: they were chosen, so election is true; it was from eternity, so eternal election is true; the persons themselves were chosen, so personal election is true; and this is a proper ground of thanksgiving, since there can be no higher reason for praise than to have been chosen to be eternally holy and happy. He guards it at once: the choice is not without respect to character but is to holiness and then to salvation, so no one has evidence of being chosen except as he has evidence of being sanctified. Henry makes the same connection: the decree connects the end and the means, which must not be separated, since we are not chosen because we were holy but that we might be holy. Clarke sets the order out as six stages, hearing the truth, believing it, receiving the Spirit, being sanctified, being saved, obtaining the glory; and he reads the choice from the beginning as the purpose to call Gentiles to the same privileges as Jews without circumcision.

The exhortation that follows is where the schools separate. Ellicott says such an exhortation is in itself conclusive against irreversible predestination, since if it were impossible for them to quit their ground it would be needless to tell them to hold it, and if they could quit it and be no worse off the charge would be needless too. Clarke argues from the sequence, that the calling did not necessarily and irresistibly lead to faith, nor faith to sanctification, nor sanctification to glory, these being stages of one journey at any of which a man might halt and never finish the race. Henry keeps doctrine and diligence together: the apostle does not say they are chosen and may therefore be careless, but that grace in election and vocation is so far from superseding our care that it should quicken us to the greatest resolution.

On the traditions to be held the same division reappears, with the roles reversed. Ellicott quotes Chrysostom with approval, that they plainly did not deliver all their tradition by letter but much besides without writing, and that both are equally worthy of belief, so that we should consider the tradition of the church worthy of belief and ask no further questions. Barnes gives five reasons why the verse furnishes no such authority: no evidence that later traditions came from the apostles, many trifling and contrary to their writings, the genuine inseparable from the false, everything necessary already in the written word, and nothing in the passage referring to anything but what the writer himself delivered. Clarke agrees it can never with propriety support traditions confessedly taken from neither Testament and spoken by neither prophet nor apostle. Henry allows the force of the verse for its own time, since the canon was not yet complete, but denies any argument from it now.
16:
The address of the prayer is what they dwell on. Barnes calls it really a prayer offered to the Saviour, language such as could be used only by one who regarded him as divine; and he turns the conjunction back on those who use it to separate them: if the word and proved Christ a different being from God it would equally prove the Father one. Calvin takes the ascription of a divine work as clear proof of Christ's divinity, and adds that we obtain nothing from God unless we seek it in him. Ellicott notices the order of the names is unusual and denies any design to prove equality, which the shared aspiration establishes only incidentally; he suggests a climax, the person whose work on the heart is more immediate being named first, the writer then watching jealously lest the Father seem less interested in our welfare than the Son. Robertson observes the participle which follows is singular, and passes on the remark that these letters probably have no instance of a plural verb where two persons of the Godhead are named together.

The consolation is defined by contrast. Barnes sets the joys of religion against every other kind: other joys fade, terminate at death, cease when sickness invades the frame or the senses in age refuse to minister as they once did; the comforts of religion depend on no such contingencies, but attend us in sickness and bereavement, are with us in death, and are unchanging beyond the grave. Henry says the same in a phrase, that the comforts of the saints are not dying things and shall not die with them. Ellicott makes it a present source of comfort of which no persecution can rob us, and reads the giving of it as the proof of the statement that he loved us.

On the hope both add the qualification. Henry grounds it on the love of God, his promise, and the experience the saints have had of his power, goodness and faithfulness, and insists that what they hope for is free grace, not their own merit. Ellicott joins the words closely, since the prospect belongs to us only in grace, all our hope resting on the continuance of strength imparted by the Father through the Son and the Spirit.

Comfort and establishment are treated as reciprocal. Henry observes that comfort is a means of establishment, since the more pleasure we take in the word and ways of God the likelier we are to persevere; and that establishment is in turn a means to comfort, since if we waver in faith or falter in duty it is no wonder we are strangers to the joys of religion. What lies at the bottom of all our uneasiness, he asks, but our unsteadiness. Clarke presses harder: it is not enough that we believe the truth, we must love it, since the faith of a devil may exist without loving obedience while a true believer's faith works by love; and against the maxim that believing the doctrines makes a man safe he sets the gospel's threefold testimony, believe, love, obey, none of which can subsist without the others.

The chapter closes with two confessions. Clarke says he has deliberately fixed no specific meaning to the apostasy, the man of sin, or the restrainer, having found it extremely difficult to satisfy himself and thinking it unlikely he could then satisfy his readers; he gives what others have said rather than attempt a new interpretation, remarking that the variety of explanations offered by wise and learned men only proves the difficulty of the place. Barnes closes with a defence: the error of the first readers concerned the time and not the fact, and the long series of events described here shows the apostles did not believe the end was near, nor teach what unbelievers have often charged them with teaching.
